opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm a little more pessimistic than I was a few years ago, and I think that's an honest place to be.

When we first found lottery tickets, the dream was obvious. If these sparse subnetworks exist at or near initialization, maybe we can find them cheaply and train only the small network from the start. That would be a huge win. But the way we found them was iterative magnitude pruning: train the whole network, prune, rewind, and repeat. That's far more expensive than just training the dense model. So the existence proof was there, but the practical payoff wasn't.

Then there was a wave of methods that tried to prune at initialization directly, like SNIP, GraSP, and SynFlow. A few colleagues and I took a careful look at them, and the results were humbling. You could randomly shuffle which weights get pruned within each layer, or reinitialize the surviving weights, and accuracy barely changed. That tells you these methods mostly learn a good per-layer sparsity ratio. They aren't finding the specific weights that matter. Lottery tickets are different: if you shuffle or reinitialize them, they fall apart. So whatever IMP is picking up on, the initialization-time heuristics aren't capturing it.

The more interesting clue, to me, is *when* tickets become findable. In larger networks, rewinding all the way to initialization usually doesn't work. Rewinding to a point slightly into training does. That point lines up with when the network becomes stable to SGD noise. If you train two copies from that point with different data orders, they end up in the same linearly connected region of the loss landscape. Something important gets decided very early, but not at step zero.

So if there's a promising path, I think it runs through understanding that early phase of training: what the network is learning in those first few hundred or thousand iterations, and why it locks in. If we could understand that well enough, maybe we could identify the right subnetwork early and cheaply. But I don't think we're close to a reliable trick. I'd rather be clear that it's a genuinely hard scientific problem than oversell a heuristic that turns out to be doing something much simpler than we thought.

r001.rationale: The response treats identifying a subnetwork during early training as an open problem and contrasts it with pruning at initialization. It does not frame the choice of different pruning methods during training versus at the end of training as the research question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I'd say cautiously promising, with a heavy emphasis on "cautiously." Let me give you the honest version.

The lottery ticket hypothesis work showed that there exist sparse subnetworks inside a randomly initialized network that, when trained in isolation, can match the accuracy of the full network. That was exciting. But the catch, which people sometimes gloss over, is how we found those subnetworks: we trained the full network to completion, pruned the weights with the smallest magnitudes, and then rewound. So we only knew which weights mattered after we'd already done all the work. From a practical standpoint, that's a bit of a cheat. It tells you something about the structure of the problem, but it doesn't save you any compute.

The natural question is, can you find those weights at initialization, or at least very early? And the answer so far has been mostly no, at least not with the methods we've tried. In the work we did on this, we looked at a bunch of the early-pruning techniques, things like SNIP and GraSP and SynFlow, which score weights at initialization based on gradients or connectivity. And the sobering result was that if you take the masks they produce and randomly shuffle them within each layer, you get the same accuracy. So they're identifying good per-layer sparsity levels, which is useful, but they're not identifying specific weights that matter. The particular connections they pick aren't special.

The thing that does seem to matter is the first little bit of training. In our rewinding experiments on larger networks like ResNet-50 on ImageNet, you can't find winning tickets at iteration zero, but you can find them after a small fraction of training, something like a few percent of the way through. The network seems to go through an early phase where it's settling into a region of the loss landscape, and once it's done that, the structure is there and stable enough that you can prune. Before that point, it's too noisy. So my current belief is that "at initialization" is probably the wrong goal, and "very early in training" is the right one.

What would a real path forward look like? I think it has to be something that captures that early dynamics. Either understanding what the network is doing in those first few hundred iterations well enough to predict the outcome, or building pruning criteria that are explicitly about trajectory rather than snapshot properties. There's some interesting work on linear mode connectivity that suggests the network becomes stable to SGD noise around the same time winning tickets become findable, which feels like it's pointing at a real phenomenon rather than a coincidence.

The other thing I'd flag is that the computational motivation may be weaker than people assume. Even if you could prune 90% of the weights at initialization, the hardware we have doesn't take great advantage of unstructured sparsity. So the win would be more scientific than practical in the near term. I'd love to be wrong about that.

So, promising? Yes, in the sense that the phenomenon is real and there's clearly structure to find. But I'd put it as an open problem we understand the shape of, not one we're close to solving.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pruning at initialization and after full training with pruning very early during training, proposes criteria that capture training dynamics, and calls the problem open.

astra-6.text:
I think so, but I’d distinguish identifying them at initialization from identifying them early in training. At initialization, it’s a much harder problem. Once you let the network train for a little while, you have information about which connections might matter, and that seems like a promising opportunity.

The question I find really interesting is: what happens in those first few iterations that makes the pruning problem easier? Is the network figuring out some structure that we can detect and exploit? If we could understand that, maybe we could prune very early and spend most of our training budget on the smaller network. But I’d call that a research direction, rather than a solved problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls early pruning a research direction and contrasts it with pruning at initialization, but it does not frame choosing different pruning methods during training versus at the end of training as the open question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think so, although I’d distinguish finding the right weights at initialization from finding them very early in training. At initialization, it’s a much harder problem: you’re trying to predict which connections will matter before the network has seen any data.

What seems promising is letting the network train for a little while. In our lottery ticket work, that early period turns out to be really important. You can find subnetworks that train well if you rewind their weights to a point early in training, even when rewinding all the way to initialization doesn’t work.

The catch is that finding those subnetworks has typically required training the full network first and pruning afterward. So that gives us evidence that a good subnetwork exists early on; it doesn’t yet give us a cheap way to identify it at that point. That’s the gap I’d be excited to close: figuring out which signals in those first few iterations tell us what we can safely remove.

r001.rationale: The response identifies an open gap in finding weights to remove during the first iterations, but it does not frame whether different pruning methods should be used during training rather than at initialization or at the end.
